etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French bronze (1511), from Italian bronzo (13th cent.), of uncertain origin; see it for more. First use appears c. 1721 in the writings of Matthew Prior. See cite below.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A naturally occurring or man-made alloy of copper, usually in combination with tin, but also with one or more other metals.

quote.citation: 1720, Matthew Prior, Poems on Several Occasions, page 339:
quote.text: How little gives thee joy or pain; A print, a bronze, a flower, a root.

definitions.definition: (countable and uncountable) A reddish-brown colour, the colour of bronze.
(countable) A work of art made of bronze, especially a sculpture.

quote.citation: 1728, [Alexander Pope], “(please specify the page)”, in The Dunciad. An Heroic Poem. […], Dublin, London:  […]  A. Dodd, →OCLC:
quote.text: Embrown'd with native bronze, lo! Henley stands.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter I, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: The house was a big elaborate limestone affair, evidently new. Winter sunshine sparkled on lace-hung casement, on glass marquise, and the burnished bronze foliations of grille and door.

definitions.definition: (of the skin) Tanned; darkened as a result of exposure to the sun.

quote.text: That girl was dynamite. Dark hair with killer blue eyes, bronze skin, and an exquisite full-figured body.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To color bronze; (of the sun) to tan.

quote.citation: 1925, DuBose Heyward, Porgy‎[1], London: Jonathan Cape, Part IV, p. 137:
quote.text: The sun was so low that its level rays shot through the tunnels of the forest and bronzed its ceiling of woven leaves when Bess returned to the clearing.

quote.citation: 1961, Freya Stark, chapter 8, in Dust in the Lion's Paw: Autobiography 1939-1946, New York: Harcourt, Brace & World, page 122:
quote.text: North is the bay of Acre, lovely in shape, and, far, far beyond, the cloudy vision of Hermon, its huge landscape now only attainable with a police pass—beautifully solitary except for good-looking young men of the police patrols, all fit and bronzed.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of the skin) To change to a bronze or tan colour due to exposure to the sun.

quote.citation: 2006, Melissa Lassor, “Out of Darkness”, in Watching Time, page 124:
quote.text: His skin began to bronze as he worked in our garden each day.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make hard or unfeeling; to brazen.

quote.citation: 1815 February 24, [Walter Scott], Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […]  James Ballantyne and Co. for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, […]; and Archibald Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: the lawyer who bronzes his bosom instead of his forehead
